title: Lesson 16 - Child FlexCards and Nested Action Flows
description: Recommend the implementation of necessary actions (e.g., links, modals, launching Omniscripts, calling Integration Procedures, Child Flexcards) on Flexcards to drive user workflows and business processes.

questions.question: A consultant wants to build a reusable detail view that can be embedded in several parent cards. What is the correct design approach?
options: Build the detail into each parent card separately
Create a child FlexCard with an explicit, self-contained data contract that receives its context from the parent
Nest the child five levels deep
Give the child a hard-coded record
questions.explanation: A reusable child FlexCard should have an explicit, self-contained data contract and receive its context from the parent, so it can be embedded in multiple parents. Duplicating the detail in each parent defeats reuse, deep nesting multiplies fetches, and a hard-coded record makes the child unusable elsewhere.

questions.question: A parent card should show a summary and let the user drill into detail without leaving the page. Which pattern is the best fit?
options: A link that navigates to a separate page
A modal that hosts a child FlexCard showing the detail
A child card with no data contract
questions.explanation: A modal that hosts a child FlexCard keeps the user in context while showing the detail, which is the drill-down pattern. A link navigates away, a text element shows no detail, and a child without a data contract has nothing to display.

questions.question: What is the main risk of nesting child FlexCards too deeply?
options: The data fetches multiply and the data contract becomes hard to trace
questions.explanation: Deep nesting multiplies data fetches and makes the data contract hard to trace, slowing the page and complicating maintenance. Reusability is a benefit, not a risk, and styling and context passing are not the primary problems with depth.
